title: How web apps keep you logged in: sessions, JWTs & refresh tokens
description: How do web apps keep you logged in, and how do they log you out? This quiz compares server-side sessions with stateless JWTs, then covers what follows from that choice: where to store tokens (`httpOnly` cookie or `localStorage`, and the XSS/CSRF tradeoff), refresh-token rotation, revocation and "log out everywhere" (the hard part of stateless auth), short-lived access tokens, and keeping multiple devices and tabs in sync. It also touches on OAuth 2.0, PKCE, and OpenID Connect. Based on RFC 7519 (JWT), RFC 6749 (OAuth 2.0), RFC 7636 (PKCE), RFC 9700 (OAuth Security BCP), and OpenID Connect Core.

questions.title: What's the main tradeoff between a stateless JWT and a server-side session?
questions.description: A server-side session keeps its state on the server and gives the client an opaque session ID. A JWT carries its own claims and is signed.

options.text: The server can check a JWT with its signature alone, with no datastore lookup per request, but it can't cancel a token before it expires.
A JWT is encrypted by default, so the client can't see its payload; a session ID is sent in plaintext.
Server-side sessions can't scale horizontally because a session only lives on the server that created it.
JWTs make HTTPS unnecessary, because the signature already stops attackers from reading or changing the token.

questions.explanation:
You trade revocation for statelessness. A standard JWT (a JWS) is *signed*, so any server with the verification key can trust its claims without a shared session store, which makes horizontal scaling easy. The cost is that there's no central record to delete. You can't kill a valid token early; it keeps working until `exp`.

The wrong answers are common misconceptions:

- A plain JWT is **base64url-encoded, not encrypted**. Anyone can decode the payload, so never put secrets in it. Use JWE if you really need encryption.
- Sessions **do** scale horizontally, with a shared store (Redis, a database) or sticky sessions.
- The signature protects *integrity*, not *confidentiality*. Without HTTPS, someone can read the token in transit and replay it, so you still need TLS.
questions.references: [RFC 7519: JSON Web Token](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519) · [OWASP: JWT for Java Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/JSON_Web_Token_for_Java_Cheat_Sheet.html)

questions.title: A JWT is three base64url segments joined by dots: `header.payload.____`. What's the third segment called?
questions.description: Type the name of the last part of a compact JWT (a JWS).
questions.explanation:
A compact JWT is `base64url(header) . base64url(payload) . signature`. The signature is computed over the encoded header and payload (for `HS256`, that's `HMAC-SHA256(base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload), secret)`). That's why tampering shows up: change one byte of the header or payload and the signature no longer verifies.

The header and payload are only encoded, though, so anyone holding the token can read them. The signature protects *integrity and authenticity*, not *confidentiality*.

questions.title: Which statements about storing an auth token in the browser are true?
questions.description: Select all that apply. Think about what JavaScript can reach and what the browser sends on its own.

options.text: Any JavaScript on the page can read a token in `localStorage`, so one XSS bug is enough to steal it.
JavaScript can't read an `httpOnly` cookie, which makes stealing the token through XSS much harder.
The browser adds cookies to matching requests automatically, and that's exactly what makes cookie-based auth vulnerable to CSRF.
Storing the token in `localStorage` instead of a cookie protects the app from both CSRF and XSS.

questions.explanation:
No storage option protects against everything. You're choosing which attack to defend against.

- **`localStorage`**: any script on the origin can read it, so XSS can steal it. The browser doesn't attach it to requests automatically, so it avoids CSRF (you send it yourself, e.g. in an `Authorization: Bearer` header).
- **`httpOnly` cookie**: JavaScript can't see it, so an XSS payload can't just read it. But the browser sends cookies along on cross-site requests automatically, and that's what CSRF exploits.

The false option swaps CSRF risk for *worse* XSS risk. It doesn't protect against both. In short: with cookies, defend against CSRF; with `localStorage`, defend against XSS. You have to defend against XSS either way, because XSS can send requests with a cookie-based session even when it can't read the cookie.
questions.references: [MDN: Using HTTP cookies — Security](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies#security) · [OWASP: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/csrf)

questions.title: You authenticate with a session cookie. What most directly prevents CSRF?
questions.description: In CSRF, an attacker gets the victim's browser to send a logged-in request the user didn't mean to send. What stops that cross-site request from carrying valid credentials, or from being accepted?

options.text: Set `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) on the cookie, and/or require an anti-CSRF token that the attacker's page can't read.
Add the `httpOnly` flag to the cookie.
Respond with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` so CORS controls every request.
Serve the site over HTTPS and enable HSTS.

questions.explanation:
CSRF works because the browser attaches the session cookie to cross-site requests *automatically*. The two standard defenses target exactly that:

- **`SameSite=Lax`/`Strict`** tells the browser not to send the cookie on cross-site requests (Lax still allows top-level GET navigations), so the forged request arrives *without* credentials.
- **Anti-CSRF tokens** (synchronizer token or double-submit) require a secret the attacker's origin can't read, so it can't build a valid request.

Why the others don't work:

- **`httpOnly`** hides the cookie from JavaScript, which is an XSS defense. CSRF doesn't need to *read* the cookie; the browser just sends it.
- **CORS** controls whether scripts can *read a cross-origin response*. It doesn't stop the request from being *sent and processed*. Forms and simple requests go through anyway, and `*` actually loosens things (and can't be used with credentials).
- **HTTPS/HSTS** protect against eavesdropping and downgrade attacks (MITM), which is a separate threat.

questions.title: With refresh-token rotation, a client sends a refresh token that was already used and replaced. What should the server do?
questions.description: With rotation, each refresh token works once: using it returns a new access token **and** a new refresh token, and the old one is retired.

options.text: Treat it as likely theft: a retired refresh token showing up again means someone has a copy, so revoke the whole token family (the session).
Quietly issue a new access token, since refresh tokens are meant to be reused as often as needed.
Accept the request but log a warning; a replay alone isn't a reason to revoke anything.
Extend the current access token without issuing a new refresh token.

questions.explanation:
This is **automatic reuse detection**, and it's the security benefit of rotation. Each refresh token works once, so there should only ever be *one* live refresh token in a family. If an old one shows up again, two parties have copies, most likely because one was stolen, and the server can't tell the thief from the real user. The safe move is to **revoke the whole family** and force a new login. That cuts off the attacker. The real user's next refresh fails too, and that's intended: when in doubt, fail closed.

The wrong answers describe non-rotating (reusable) refresh tokens or a log-and-allow approach. Both throw away the reason for rotating in the first place. RFC 9700 recommends rotation with reuse detection for public clients, which can't keep a client secret.

questions.title: Why are access tokens short-lived (minutes) while refresh tokens last for days?
questions.description: Access tokens are sent with every API call. Refresh tokens are exchanged now and then to get new access tokens.

options.text: You can't revoke a stateless access token instantly, so a short lifetime limits how long a leaked one works. The refresh step is where revocation checks actually happen.
A shorter expiry makes the signature cryptographically stronger and harder to forge.
Short-lived tokens are physically smaller, which noticeably reduces request bandwidth.
A short lifetime prevents CSRF because the token expires before an attacker can use it.

questions.explanation:
Short-lived access tokens **limit the damage** from a leak. A stateless JWT is accepted on its signature alone, so you can't reliably cancel it early. With a 5-15 minute lifetime, a stolen access token stops working soon after it's taken. The long-lived refresh token, meanwhile, has to *pass through a checkpoint you control*. Each refresh is a chance to check server state: Is the user disabled? Did they log out? Was the family revoked? So revocation takes effect within about one access-token lifetime.

The wrong answers mix in unrelated things. Expiry has nothing to do with signature strength (that depends on the algorithm and key) or token size (the `exp` claim is a few bytes either way). CSRF is about the browser sending credentials automatically, not about how long a token lives.

questions.title: You use stateless JWT access tokens and need "log out everywhere" to work quickly. Which approaches do that?
questions.description: Select every approach that really makes existing access tokens stop working soon. Look for what the working ones have in common.

options.text: Keep access tokens short-lived and revoke the refresh tokens. Active access tokens expire within one short lifetime.
Keep a server-side denylist of revoked token IDs (`jti`) and check it on every request.
Store a token version per user, and reject any token with an older version after you increase it.
Have the server delete the JWT from the user's browser `localStorage`.

questions.explanation:
What the three correct answers share: **to revoke a stateless token, you have to add some state back.** A signature check alone can't know a token is unwanted, so every approach that works adds a lookup:

- **Short lifetime + revoked refresh tokens**: the cheapest. You accept a short window (the access-token lifetime) and skip per-request denylist checks.
- **`jti` denylist**: precise and immediate, but every request now does a revocation lookup (usually cached). You've partly rebuilt sessions.
- **Token version (`tokenVersion` claim)**: increasing the user's version invalidates all their tokens at once ("log out everywhere"), but you have to read the current version on each request.

The false option can't work: a server **can't reach into a browser's `localStorage`**, and even if it could, the attacker may have copied the token somewhere else. Revocation has to happen where the token is *checked* (the server), not where it's *stored* (the client).

questions.title: What does OpenID Connect (OIDC) add to OAuth 2.0?
questions.description: A common interview trap: OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are related, but they solve different problems.

options.text: An identity layer: a signed **ID Token** (a JWT) describing the logged-in user, plus a standard `/userinfo` endpoint. OAuth 2.0 on its own handles authorization, not authentication.
Required encryption for every access token the authorization server issues.
Long-lived API keys that replace OAuth's access tokens.
No more redirect-based authorization step, so the browser round-trip goes away.

questions.title: Why do public clients (SPAs, mobile apps) use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE instead of the old Implicit flow?
questions.description: PKCE stands for Proof Key for Code Exchange. The client creates a random `code_verifier`, sends its hash as `code_challenge` at the start, and reveals the verifier when it redeems the code.

options.text: PKCE ties the authorization code to a secret only the original client knows (`code_verifier`), so a stolen code is useless. The Implicit flow put tokens directly in the redirect URL, where they leak.
PKCE lets a public client safely include a long-lived client secret in its shipped code.
The Implicit flow is actually more secure, and PKCE gives up some of that security for faster logins.
PKCE encrypts the access token end to end so the browser never sees it in cleartext.

questions.explanation:
Public clients can't keep a client secret (anyone can read an SPA's JavaScript or decompile an app), so the usual protection for confidential clients isn't available. PKCE replaces it with a **new secret for each request**:

```text
code_verifier  = random high-entropy string (kept in the client)
code_challenge = base64url(SHA-256(code_verifier))   // sent on the authorize request
```

The authorization server saves the `code_challenge` and sends a code back through the redirect. The token endpoint then requires the matching `code_verifier`. An attacker who intercepts the *code* (say, through a malicious app registered for the same custom URI scheme, or from browser history) still can't redeem it without the verifier.

The **Implicit flow** returned the access token directly in the URL fragment (`#access_token=...`). That exposed it to browser history, logs, and referrer leaks, with no exchange step to protect it. That's why current guidance (RFC 9700) is Authorization Code + PKCE for every client, and no Implicit flow. The wrong answers misdescribe PKCE: it doesn't let you store a secret, it isn't a security downgrade, and it doesn't encrypt tokens.
questions.references: [RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7636) · [RFC 9700 §2.1: Protecting Redirect-Based Flows](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9700#section-2.1)

questions.title: Your servers validate JWTs and sometimes reject *freshly issued* tokens as "not yet valid" or "expired", depending on which server handles the request. What's the likely cause and fix?
questions.description: The errors come from the `nbf` (not before) and `exp` (expiration) claims, and they depend on *which* server validates the token, not on how old the token is.

options.text: Clock skew between the issuer and the validating servers. Allow a small leeway when checking `exp`/`nbf`, and keep all clocks in sync with NTP.
The signing key was rotated; re-sign every outstanding token.
The tokens are over the maximum JWT size; make the payload smaller.
CORS preflight requests delay calls until after expiry; turn off CORS.

questions.explanation:
`exp` and `nbf` are **absolute timestamps** (NumericDate: seconds since the Unix epoch), and each server compares them against its *own* clock. If the issuer's clock runs a few seconds ahead, a server with a slower clock sees a brand-new token's `nbf` as still in the future: "not yet valid." The reverse happens too: a server with a fast clock sees a nearly expired token as already past `exp`. The giveaway here is that the result depends on *which server* validates, not on how much time has passed.

The standard fix has two parts:

1. **Sync clocks** with NTP so drift stays tiny.
2. **Allow a small leeway** (a few seconds up to a couple of minutes) when checking `exp`/`nbf`. Most JWT libraries have a `clockTolerance` or `leeway` option for this. RFC 7519 allows "some small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, to account for clock skew."

The other answers don't match the symptom. A rotated key causes *signature* failures, not time errors. Size limits show up as transport or header errors. CORS has nothing to do with checking `exp`/`nbf`.

questions.title: Your SPA is open in three tabs. One tab refreshes the access token, which rotates the refresh token. How should the other tabs avoid using a stale token *and* avoid all refreshing at once?
questions.description: All tabs share the same origin and the same stored tokens. With rotation, the old refresh token works only once.

options.text: Coordinate between tabs, for example with a `BroadcastChannel`/`storage` event or a Web Lock, so one tab does the refresh and the others pick up the new token.
Let every tab refresh on its own at the same time; rotation will sort out the duplicates.
Move token storage to `sessionStorage` so each tab keeps its own separate token.
Turn off refresh-token rotation so simultaneous refreshes don't cause problems.

questions.explanation:
With rotation, **refreshing from several tabs at once is dangerous**, and this is where it bites in practice. If two tabs use the *same* refresh token at the same time, the second one presents a token that was already rotated. Reuse detection treats that as theft and **revokes the whole family**, which logs the user out of every tab. The fix is to coordinate between tabs:

- a **Web Lock** (`navigator.locks.request`) so only one tab holds the refresh lock at a time, or
- a **`BroadcastChannel`** or the `storage` event to pick one tab to refresh and send the new token to the rest (often combined with a single shared in-memory promise, so overlapping calls wait for one network request).

Each wrong answer backfires. Tabs refreshing at the same time is exactly what triggers reuse detection. `sessionStorage` is per tab, so tabs wouldn't share a login at all. Turning off rotation removes the race only by giving up the security you added rotation for.

questions.title: Which registered JWT claim uniquely identifies a single token, making it the natural key for a revocation denylist?
questions.description: Type the three-letter claim name from RFC 7519's registered claims.
questions.explanation:
`jti` is the **JWT ID**, a value that uniquely identifies the token and "can be used to prevent the JWT from being replayed" (RFC 7519 §4.1.7). Since it's unique per token, it works well as the key for a revocation **denylist**: store the `jti` of any token you want to kill (until its `exp`; after that it expires anyway) and reject matching tokens on each request.

The catch: checking a `jti` denylist on every request adds back server state and a lookup per request. You've partly rebuilt the session you were trying to avoid, which is the tension that keeps coming up with stateless auth (see the "log out everywhere" question). For precise, immediate revocation, that's often worth it.
